extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, patent examiners, and courts considering patent appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and procedural rules governing appeals from the Commissioner of Patents concerning priority of invention, reduction to practice, evidentiary rules for contested patent proceedings, caveats, abandonment/public-use bars, and joint-invention issues under the 1836 and 1839 Patent Acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: First inventor / priority of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The first inventor is prima facie entitled to a patent; generally the first of two original inventors who communicates the invention to the public is entitled to the patent, although the other may have invented earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine originates in Dolland's case and subsequent decisions: public communication/ disclosure gives priority. However, where a prior inventor is bona fide and using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting his invention (and preparing to apply), he should not be defeated by a subsequent inventor who first obtains a patent. Whether delay or concealment amounts to forfeiture/abandonment is a question of fact for a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'reduced to practice' generally means bringing the invention into such form that it may be used and is not a mere theory; a machine described so it may be made and used, and especially if a model is made, may be said to be reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing the specification, drawings, and a model as required by statute may suffice where the nature of the case admits of drawings or a model. Actual construction of a model or small working example demonstrates practicability; size is immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat filing: nature and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat does not create any right; it is simply a request to be favored with information and only enables the filer to have notice of any interfering application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caveat gives notice to the Commissioner only and is kept confidential in the office; it does not give notice to the world or to the interfering applicant, and its omission does not impair the filer's title nor does its presence make the patent judged differently when granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay is not per se fatal; abandonment is the key
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not limit the time to apply for a patent; delay is unimportant unless it amounts to evidence of abandonment of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay, lapse of time, or taking long to apply does not automatically forfeit rights unless there is intervening public use or other evidence of abandonment or dedication to the public. Determination of intent behind delay and whether delay constituted abandonment is a question of fact for a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use / two-year statutory bar
rubrics_metrics.description: If the thing invented has been in public use or publicly sold with the consent of the applicant for more than two years prior to application, that use may be a bar to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the referenced acts (e.g., 15th section of 1836 and 7th section of 1839), a defendant in infringement litigation may defend by showing the machine was in public use with the patentee's consent for more than two years prior to application; such use may defeat the right to a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's rules for taking and transmitting evidence (Rules 1–5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner promulgated binding rules for contested proceedings: (1) statements and evidence must be in writing and verified by oath/affirmation; (2) all statements/evidence must be filed in the Patent Office before the hearing; (3) notice of depositions must be given to the opposite party in sufficient time and proof of service attached so the opposite party can cross-examine; (4) no evidence will be considered at the hearing unless taken and filed in compliance with the rules, except where good reasons are shown for inability to procure testimony; (5) all evidence shall be sealed up and addressed to the Commissioner and certified accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules, made pursuant to statutory authority, bind the Commissioner as much as statute while they remain in force. They apply especially to contested cases and secure fair opportunity to cross-examine and guard against tampering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence not taken/filed per rules will not be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence, statement, or declaration touching the matter at issue will be considered at the hearing which has not been taken and filed in compliance with the Commissioner's rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is provision to notify the Commissioner in advance if a party is unable for good reasons to procure testimony within the stipulated time; otherwise failure to comply is fatal to consideration of that evidence. The rule is an assurance by the Commissioner that he will not consider noncompliant evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sealing requirement for depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions must be sealed up by the magistrate before whom they were taken and the magistrate must certify that they were sealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification that a deposition was sealed is a non‑immaterial form and is a security against alteration after the deposition left the magistrate. Absence of certification is sufficient ground for excluding the deposition from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to cross-examine
rubrics_metrics.description: Before taking a deposition, notice must be given to the opposite party of the time and place so the opposite party or counsel has full opportunity to cross-examine the witness; proof of service of notice must be attached to the deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short notice may be excused where the opposite party actually appears and cross-examines, but lateness might justify seeking additional time to take countervailing testimony. The rule secures fairness in contested proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence of witnesses: interest disqualifies
rubrics_metrics.description: If a witness is interested, he is excluded; no man can be a witness in his own cause unless made competent by statute or called by the opposing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a small amount of interest may render a witness incompetent. However, issues of interest may go to credibility and admissibility depending on the precise nature and certainty of the interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner bound by his rules; cannot dispense arbitrarily
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules promulgated by the Commissioner under statutory authority are binding while in force and the Commissioner has not reserved a right to dispense with them in particular cases at his pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A dispensation by the Commissioner cannot affect depositions already taken while rules were in force; revocation of the rules affects only subsequent proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence and legal sufficiency of evidence is for the parties to insist upon
rubrics_metrics.description: After a contest arises, parties have a right to insist that evidence be taken according to the rules and that it be evidence 'competent in law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections to evidence on grounds of competency, interest, improper procedure, or noncompliance with rules are proper and may lead to exclusion; courts must enforce these standards in contested cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must be the inventor (statutory requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the statute (6th section referenced), the applicant must be the inventor; a person who is not the sole inventor cannot properly be granted a patent as sole applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where applications show joint invention or the applicant is not the true inventor, the Commissioner may withhold or refuse to grant a patent. The statutory requirement gives the Commissioner authority to deny patents when the applicant fails to meet the inventor condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint invention: neither party may claim the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is a joint invention, neither of the parties can claim the whole and the Commissioner may reject applications seeking exclusive whole rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows that principle/discovery and reduction to practice involved contributions from multiple persons (e.g., discovery of principle by one and reduction to practice by another), none may be entitled to a sole patent; joint rights or rejection may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine separating secret (closet) invention from public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who confines an invention to his closet and doesn't communicate it to the public may forfeit priority to a subsequent inventor who communicates it; the former is treated as having abandoned public claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dolland's case is cited: withholding the discovery from the public and taking no steps toward patenting until another obtains a patent may be treated as abandonment; questions of forfeiture or abandonment are questions of fact for a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when patent refused: equity bill
rubrics_metrics.description: Where patents are refused by the Commissioner (or on appeal), the applicant may have remedy by bill in equity; the court may adjudge that the applicant is entitled to a patent and authorize the Commissioner to issue it upon filing a copy of the adjudication and complying with requisitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparison of the 1836 and 1839 acts shows statutory provision for equitable remedies and judicial adjudication to resolve rights where administrative denial is contested.
